extracted.intended_audience: scholars/students of medieval natural philosophy and history of science; readers of Latin treatises on 'mirabilia'
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing principles, classifications, and procedural recipes given in a medieval Latin treatise on marvels (natural properties, sympathies/antipathies, remedies, instruments, and geometric methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of marvels (septem modis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mirabilia (marvels) are distinguished into seven kinds: those that happen by nature, by bodily powers, by ingenuity (ingenii), by property, by certain (extraordinary) powers, because the cause is hidden and produced by craft (artificium), or simply (sine speciali causa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text enumerates and exemplifies these seven modes and notes where particular examples fall (e.g., some phenomena are natural, others produced by craft or hidden causes). The author uses this taxonomy to decide whether to attribute a marvel to natural forces, human artifice, faith/charms, or unknown causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy and antipathy as causal principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects can arise from sympathy (consensus/affinity) or antipathy between things; sympathy produces concordant effects without manifest reason, antipathy the contrary (e.g., animals reacting to certain persons or smells).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous exempla are given (wolves and humans, animals and odors, stones and animals). Sympathy is treated as a hidden but efficacious cause; sometimes it operates without manifest reason. The text warns that such occurrences may be frequent but not universal and recommends examining particular cases (occasional counterexamples are discussed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacy depends on body, application site and disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicinal or wondrous effects of substances (e.g., 'mumia', buried parts, specific concoctions) depend on the place of application, the state of the body, and other contingent factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a mummy (resinous funerary preparation) is medicinal when applied to a suitable place; some remedies are effective only in particular local applications. The author cautions that not every instance will work for every person or case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dietary and pharmacological qualities influence memory, temperament, and offspring
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain foods, herbs, and preparations (melissa, gallinacean parts, seeds, eggs, testudines, camel substances) are asserted to strengthen memory, wit, courage, and may affect the intellect or the disposition of offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links specific substances to mental faculties (e.g., melissa improves memory and acumen; some womb-foods influence children's talents). It gives examples, mentions endorsements by authorities (e.g., Galen, Symeon), and notes that effects may vary by regimen and quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of odors, tactile forms and tattoos to influence animal behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Odors and physical marks can influence animals' perceptions and behavior (e.g., odours applied to horses to arouse or repel them; tattoos/paint affect horses' reactions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims include that odor/shape can make animals perceive sex or react despite visual deficiency; the author cites examples and speculates on mechanisms (odor perception, familiar smell). Practical notes: odors and fashioning of objects can be used intentionally, but not all reported effects are certain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters, names, and ritual actions may produce effects when faith and proper rites are present
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscriptions, characters ('characteres'), recitations, sacrificial acts and ritual forms are described as means to effect changes (binding, averting, conjuring), sometimes relying on the faith of participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text distinguishes licit usages (some parts may be lawful) and cautions against superstition; it observes that effectiveness often depends on faith, proper performance, and may be indistinguishable from natural causes in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric/proportional construction to determine distances and latitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for using circles, meridians, and proportional relations of periphery to diameter to compute distances, latitudes, and altitudes of places—by fixing meridian circle, using mobile circles, dividing circumferences and using proportional arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author gives a multi-step construction: fix a meridian circle, mark poles and vertex, place additional circles with movable pegs, divide peripheries into parts, and use arcs and proportional relations (reference to Archimedes and Ptolemy). Notes that numeric precision helps but perfect cognition may be difficult; offers concrete geometric operations rather than just assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical counting device for measuring paces/steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Design for a mechanical instrument: a wheel with teeth engaging a drum with a detachable peg so that after a fixed number of wheel revolutions a small stone or pellet drops into a receptacle—converting wheel revolutions into counted paces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit numerical example is given (wheel circumference measured in paces, teeth count, iterations producing counts of thousands of paces). This is presented as an artificer's method to obtain exact measurements (practical engineering recipe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes and cures of dreams and sleeplessness
rubrics_metrics.description: Dreams arise from various causes: heavy or obstructive humors, hot/dry or cold/wet qualities, vapors, certain foods and drinks, and mental agitation; remedies include preventing the causing material, applying substances to arteries (e.g., camphor with vinegar) to promote wakefulness, and removing inducing causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text classifies dreams (terrifying, minor), links them to physical humors and vapors, and prescribes anti-dream measures (e.g., camphor and vinegar on arteries promotes vigilance). It advises considering both dietary causes and corporeal agitation when treating dreams; warns that some dream-signs foreshadow misfortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burial or placing of animal parts can affect growth, soil or human condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that burying parts of animals (ram's horn, wolf tail, intestines, etc.) or placing them near plants/fields changes fertility, growth rate, or produces other effects (e.g., improving asparagus, repelling flies, accelerating fruiting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many exempla are offered, sometimes with caution about reliability. The author records folk practice and testimonies, notes probable natural or sympathetic explanations, and sometimes questions universality of such effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathetic contagion and transference in remedies and marvels
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that properties of one body can be transferred to another through contact, ingestion, burial, or preparation (e.g., 'mumia' from corpses used medicinally; ingestion or contact with parts transmits virtue or poison).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous examples: Egyptian 'mumia' used as medicine, animal-eaten stones, poultices made from specific parts. The text also advises caution: some traditions may be false, and usage must consider purity, place of application, and dosage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical precision sometimes unnecessary but useful for exact knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric measurement (numerus) is not always necessary for efficacy, but precise numerical/proportional relations (e.g., periphery to diameter, divisions of circles) enable exact understanding and instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author remarks that while number is not always required (practical operations may work without exact counts), achieving perfect cognition of some phenomena (especially geometric/astronomical) benefits from precise measures and proportion; he balances practical craft with mathematical demonstration.
